knowledgePoints.name: Code that runs vs. a request that might be honoured
knowledgePoints.teach:
Programmatic enforcement guarantees deterministic compliance; prompt instructions are probabilistic and have a non-zero failure rate.

A hook is code that runs. A prompt is a request. If a rule must hold on every run — including the ones nobody is watching — it belongs in a hook.

This is the answer to the exam's most-quoted sample question. An agent skips get_customer in 12% of cases before issuing refunds. The fix is a programmatic prerequisite that blocks lookup_order and process_refund until identity is verified — not more few-shot examples, not a stronger instruction, not a better model.

Twelve percent is not a prompting problem. Twelve percent is what "usually" looks like at scale.

questions.q: An agent skips identity verification in 12% of refunds. What class of fix actually closes the gap?
options: Add few-shot examples showing verification first
A programmatic prerequisite that blocks the refund tools until identity is verified
Move the instruction to the top of the system prompt
questions.explain: Every option except the hook leaves a residual failure rate. The whole point of the principle is that "almost always" is a different category from "always."

questions.q: Which requirement most clearly belongs in a hook rather than a prompt?
options: Prefer a friendly tone with frustrated customers
Never issue a refund without a verified customer identity
Summarise long documents before quoting them
Ask clarifying questions when the request is vague
questions.explain: Three of these are judgment, which prompts are good at. One is an invariant, which prompts cannot guarantee.

reviewQuestions.q: State the principle in one sentence.
options: A hook is code that runs; a prompt is a request — invariants belong in hooks
Prompts should always be replaced by hooks
Hooks are for tools, prompts are for text
reviewQuestions.explain: Glossary t9. Note the limit: judgment still belongs in the prompt.

knowledgePoints.name: The event list
knowledgePoints.teach:
Python HookEvent: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact, Notification, SubagentStart, PermissionRequest. The TypeScript SDK supports additional events beyond these.

Group them by what they are about and the list stops being a list:

  • Per tool call — PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PermissionRequest
  • Per turn — UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop
  • Per agent / session — SubagentStart, PreCompact, Notification

questions.q: You want code to run every time the agent tries to end its turn. Which event?
questions.explain: Stop fires when the agent attempts to finish — which is what makes it the place to demand evidence before it can.

questions.q: Which event fires when a tool call has already failed?
questions.explain: A distinct event, so recovery logic does not have to live inside the success path.

reviewQuestions.q: Which of these is NOT a Python HookEvent?
reviewQuestions.explain: The one that sounds plausible is the invented one. PostToolUse is what you would use for that moment.

knowledgePoints.name: HookMatcher and the callback signature
knowledgePoints.teach:
Hooks go in the hooks option, keyed by event, as a list of matchers:

HookMatcher(
    matcher="Bash",        # tool name or pattern, e.g. "Write|Edit"; omit to match all
    hooks=[my_callback],
    timeout=None,          # seconds; default 600, except UserPromptSubmit at 30
)

The callback is (input, tool_use_id, context) -> HookJSONOutput. input is a discriminated union on hook_event_name.

All hook inputs share session_id, transcript_path, cwd and an optional permission_mode. PreToolUseHookInput adds tool_name, tool_input, tool_use_id — and, when firing inside a subagent, agent_id and agent_type.

questions.q: Write the matcher that runs a hook on Write and Edit but not Read.
options: Omit matcher and filter inside the callback
questions.explain: A pattern string. Omitting the matcher matches every tool, which is the blunt version.

questions.q: Which fields let a hook know it is firing inside a subagent rather than the main thread?
questions.explain: They appear on PreToolUseHookInput specifically when the call originates inside a subagent.

knowledgePoints.name: Command hooks and exit codes
knowledgePoints.teach:
Hooks can also be shell commands configured in settings files rather than callbacks in your code. For those:

  • Exit code 2 blocks the action and feeds stderr back to Claude.
  • Stderr from a hook that exits 0 goes only to the debug log — Claude never sees it.

That second rule explains a common confusion: "my hook printed a warning and the model ignored it." It did not ignore it. It never received it.

questions.q: A command hook prints a warning to stderr and exits 0. What does Claude see?
options: The warning, injected next to the tool result
Nothing — stderr from an exit-0 hook goes only to the debug log
The warning as a system message
questions.explain: Exit 0 means "fine, carry on." If you want the model to read it, exit 2 and block.

questions.q: Which exit code blocks the action and sends stderr to Claude?
questions.explain: Specifically 2. Other non-zero codes are treated as hook failure rather than a deliberate block.

reviewQuestions.q: What is the default hook timeout, and which event differs?
reviewQuestions.explain: 600s default, UserPromptSubmit at 30 — because a user is sitting there waiting.

knowledgePoints.name: Out vs. back
knowledgePoints.teach:
PreToolUse guards what goes out. PostToolUse cleans what comes back.

Direction is the whole distinction, and it decides almost every hook question on the exam. Two named patterns:

  • Tool call interception hook (glossary t11) — intercepts an outgoing call to enforce a business rule. Canonical case: block process_refund over $500 and redirect to human escalation. That is PreToolUse with permissionDecision: "deny" and a reason — or updatedInput to rewrite it.
  • PostToolUse normalization (t10) — intercepts results to transform them before the model reads them. Canonical case: several MCP tools return timestamps in different formats (Unix epoch, ISO 8601, MM/DD/YYYY) and a hook normalises them so the model never has to reconcile the mismatch.

questions.q: Several MCP tools return timestamps in different formats. Where do you fix it?
options: In the system prompt, explaining each format
A PostToolUse hook that normalises the results
A PreToolUse hook that rewrites the request
By merging the tools into one
questions.explain: "Different tools return inconsistent formats" is the tell for PostToolUse. Asking the model to reconcile formats is work it should never have to do.

questions.q: Block any refund over $500 and route it to a human. Which hook?
options: PreToolUse, denying the outgoing call with a reason
Stop, refusing to end the turn
questions.explain: You want the refund never to happen, not to be detected afterwards. That means intercepting on the way out.

reviewQuestions.q: Give the one-line rule for choosing between PreToolUse and PostToolUse.
options: Pre for cheap checks, Post for expensive ones
Pre guards what goes out; Post cleans what comes back
Pre for MCP tools, Post for built-ins
reviewQuestions.explain: Direction. And note the last option is wrong — PostToolUse can block with decision: "block".

knowledgePoints.name: Two return shapes, split by event
knowledgePoints.teach:
EventsPatternKey fields
PreToolUsehookSpecificOutputpermissionDecision: allow / deny / ask / defer, plus permissionDecisionReason
PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompacttop-level decisiondecision: "block", reason
PermissionRequesthookSpecificOutputdecision.behavior: allow / deny
SessionStart, SubagentStartcontext onlyadditionalContext; no blocking
Notification, SessionEnd, PostCompact, InstructionsLoadednoneside effects only — logging, cleanup

Getting the shape wrong is silent: a PostToolUse hook that returns permissionDecision is returning a field that event does not read.

questions.q: Your PostToolUse hook returns hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision: "deny". What happens?
options: Nothing useful — PostToolUse reads a top-level decision: "block", not permissionDecision
questions.explain: Wrong shape for the event, and it fails quietly. PostToolUse blocks via the top-level decision field.

questions.q: Which events can only add context and never block?
questions.explain: They fire before there is anything to block. additionalContext is all they offer.

knowledgePoints.name: The four PreToolUse decisions
knowledgePoints.teach:
permissionDecision takes four values, and they are not two pairs:

  • allow — proceed, skipping the rest of the permission flow.
  • deny — refuse, with permissionDecisionReason fed back so the model can adapt rather than retry blindly.
  • ask — fall through to the normal prompt / canUseTool.
  • defer — park the call and hand it to your application.

Always supply permissionDecisionReason on a deny. A denial without a reason teaches the model nothing, and it will usually try again.

questions.q: Why does a deny need permissionDecisionReason?
options: The reason is fed back to the model so it can adapt instead of retrying blindly
It is required for the exit code to be honoured
questions.explain: A denial is a teaching moment. Without the reason, you get the same call again with different phrasing.

questions.q: Which permissionDecision value hands the call back to the normal permission flow?
questions.explain: ask says "I have no opinion, use the usual rules." defer is different — it parks the call for your own UI.

reviewQuestions.q: Which field does a Stop hook use to prevent the agent ending its turn?
reviewQuestions.explain: Stop is in the top-level-decision family, alongside PostToolUse and UserPromptSubmit.

knowledgePoints.name: updatedInput and additionalContext
knowledgePoints.teach:
Denial is not the only move. Two fields let a hook fix instead of refuse:

  • PreToolUse → updatedInput (directly under hookSpecificOutput) replaces the tool's arguments before it runs. Use it when the call is nearly right — a missing tenant filter, an unscoped path, a limit that is too high.
  • PostToolUse → additionalContext injects a string into Claude's context, wrapped in a system reminder, placed next to the tool result. Capped at 10,000 characters; longer output is written to a file and replaced with a preview and the path.

Rewriting is usually kinder than denying: the model gets a working result rather than a rejection it has to reason its way around.

questions.q: An agent keeps calling a search tool without the tenant filter. Deny, or rewrite?
options: Deny with a reason, so the model learns
Rewrite with updatedInput, adding the filter before the call runs
Block in PostToolUse after seeing the leaked results
questions.explain: The call is nearly right. Rewriting gets the work done and closes the hole; denial just costs a turn.

questions.q: What is the cap on additionalContext, and what happens beyond it?
options: 1,000 characters; the rest is truncated silently
10,000 characters; longer output is written to a file and replaced with a preview and path
questions.explain: 10,000 characters, with a spill-to-file fallback so nothing is lost — the model just has to go and read it.

reviewQuestions.q: Which field replaces a tool's arguments before the tool runs?
reviewQuestions.explain: updatedInput, on PreToolUse. updatedPermissions is a canUseTool field and does something else.

knowledgePoints.name: Parking a call for a human
knowledgePoints.teach:
A PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision: "defer" produces:

  • stop_reason: "tool_deferred"
  • the pending call in deferred_tool_use

That is how you surface an approval request in your own UI — a manager approving a refund in your web app, not in a terminal — and resume later with the same session_id.

Contrast with ask, which hands the decision to the SDK's own permission flow, and with deny, which ends the matter.

questions.q: A manager must approve a refund in your web UI before the tool runs. Which decision value?
questions.explain: ask routes to the SDK's permission flow. defer hands the pending call to you.

questions.q: What stop_reason accompanies a deferred tool call?
questions.explain: A dedicated stop_reason, with the pending call in deferred_tool_use so you know what you are approving.

reviewQuestions.q: After a deferred call is approved, how do you continue?
options: Start a new query with the same prompt
Call the tool yourself and inject the result
reviewQuestions.explain: Same session, picked up where it stopped.

knowledgePoints.name: Six modes
knowledgePoints.teach:
ModeBehaviour
defaultStandard prompting behaviour
acceptEditsAuto-accept file edits
planRead-only; explore and propose without editing
dontAskNever prompt — deny anything not pre-approved
bypassPermissionsSkip checks (explicit ask rules still prompt); requires allowDangerouslySkipPermissions: true
autoA model classifier approves or denies what would have been prompts

The pair worth drilling is dontAsk versus bypassPermissions: one denies everything unapproved, the other allows almost everything. They sound similar and are opposites.

questions.q: A nightly unattended agent must never prompt and never do anything you did not pre-approve. Which mode?
questions.explain: dontAsk: no prompts, and anything not pre-approved is denied. bypassPermissions also never prompts — by allowing instead.

questions.q: What does bypassPermissions still honour?
options: Explicit ask rules, which still prompt
questions.explain: And scoped disallowedTools rules like "Bash(rm *)" also still deny — bypass is not total.

reviewQuestions.q: dontAsk vs. bypassPermissions in one line each.
options: Both skip prompts and allow everything
dontAsk never prompts and denies anything unapproved; bypassPermissions skips checks and allows
reviewQuestions.explain: Same silence, opposite defaults. A classic confusable pair.

knowledgePoints.name: canUseTool only fires on a prompt
knowledgePoints.teach:
canUseTool is the SDK replacement for the interactive permission prompt. It is invoked only when the permission flow resolves to a prompt.

Calls already approved by allowedTools, by a settings allow rule, or by a permissive permissionMode (acceptEdits, bypassPermissions) never reach it.

To gate every tool call unconditionally, use a PreToolUse hook, not canUseTool.

Exceptions that reach canUseTool even when otherwise allowed: AskUserQuestion, MCP tools marked requiresUserInteraction, and connector tools an organisation set to ask. In dontAsk mode those are denied instead of prompting.

It returns a PermissionResult: { behavior: "allow", updatedInput?, updatedPermissions? } or { behavior: "deny", message, interrupt? }.

questions.q: You log every tool call from canUseTool and the log has holes. Why?
options: Calls approved by allowedTools, settings rules, or a permissive mode never reach it
Logging must be async or entries are dropped
questions.explain: It is a prompt replacement, not an interceptor. An audit trail belongs in PreToolUse.

questions.q: Which of these reaches canUseTool even when the tool would otherwise be allowed?
questions.explain: AskUserQuestion, MCP tools marked requiresUserInteraction, and org-set-to-ask connector tools are the three exceptions.

reviewQuestions.q: canUseTool vs. a PreToolUse hook — what is the difference in when they fire?
options: canUseTool fires on every call; PreToolUse only on writes
canUseTool fires only when the flow resolves to a prompt; PreToolUse fires on every call
PreToolUse fires only in default mode
reviewQuestions.explain: Another confusable pair, and the reason audit and enforcement code belongs in the hook.

knowledgePoints.name: allowedTools auto-approves; it does not restrict
knowledgePoints.teach:
allowedTools does not restrict.

It auto-approves the tools it lists. Unlisted tools do not become unavailable — they fall through to permissionMode and canUseTool. Depending on the mode, an unlisted tool may prompt, be denied, or simply run.

To actually block, use disallowedTools, which has two modes of its own:

  • A bare "Bash" removes the tool from Claude's context entirely — it is not in the tool list, so it is never considered.
  • A scoped rule like "Bash(rm *)" leaves the tool available and denies matching calls in every mode, including bypassPermissions.

questions.q: You put only Read and Grep in allowedTools, in default mode. Can the agent write a file?
options: Yes — Write falls through to the permission mode, which may prompt or allow it
No — unlisted tools are removed from context
Only if a hook allows it
questions.explain: The single most common misreading in this whole section. Auto-approval is not restriction.

questions.q: Which rule still denies matching calls under bypassPermissions?
questions.explain: Scoped disallow rules survive bypass. A bare "Bash" would remove the tool entirely, which also works but costs you the tool.

reviewQuestions.q: What is the difference between disallowedTools: ["Bash"] and disallowedTools: ["Bash(rm *)"]?
options: No difference; the second is just more specific
The bare name removes the tool from context; the scoped rule keeps the tool and denies matching calls in every mode
The scoped rule only applies in default mode
The bare name prompts; the scoped rule denies
reviewQuestions.explain: One takes the tool away, the other polices it. Both are real restriction, unlike allowedTools.
